newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Plan to censure EU Commission gains ground.
newsitem.headline: Plan to censure EU Commission gains ground.

text.p: The European Commission must implement measures by the end of the year to correct serious mistakes made in the mad cow crisis, or face a censure motion, the head of a European Parliament inquiry said on Thursday.
A censure motion, which requires a two-thirds majority vote, would force the resignation of President Jacques Santer and the 20 EU commissioners.
The parliament is due to vote on February 19 on the inquiry's report and the recommendation to warn the Commission it will face a censure motion in December if it does not toe the line.

"There has been major mishandling (of the BSE crisis) which requires corrective measures but we must realise that the Commission is not mainly responsible," German Christian Democrat Reimer Boege told a news conference.
Boege was referring to Britain where the first case of the fatal cattle brain disease bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) was reported in 1986.
Since then over 165,000 British cattle have been struck down with the disease, compared with about 300 in the rest of Europe.
In March 1996, the British government admitted that BSE could be passed to people who ate infected beef, triggering a confidence crisis among consumers and sending prices crashing.
Listing measures that the EU's executive must take this year, Boege said it must firstly reorganise its veterinary services.
Control of human and animal health should be transferred to its fledgling consumer service from its all-powerful agricultural division.
Scientific advisory committees should be more professionally managed, greater account taken of minority views and formal votes held at the end of meetings, he added.
The Commission must ensure that EU rules banning the use of meat and bone meal in animal feed were properly enforced.
The measures listed by Boege largely reiterated changes outlined to the committee by Commission President Jacques Santer in Strasbourg on January 15.
They are much weaker than radical deputies would like.
A Commission spokesman said that decisions would be announced before next month's parliament vote.

"For the moment the Commission is quite serene on this matter," the spokesman said, adding that the committee of inquiry was still discussing the issue and the Commission would comment only after the parliament had taken a decision.
The committee is split over what action to take.

French Socialist Andre Laignel, a leading member of the committee, told reporters that the Commission should take Britain to the European Court of Justice to make it compensate other member states for BSE losses, estimated at 1.6 billion Ecus in 1996.
Belgian Socialist Jose Happart, the most radical member of the 19-member cross-party committee, said on Thursday he would seek the 63 votes required for for an immediate vote of censure.
"A conditional censure makes no sense," he told a news briefing, "How many deaths are needed before parliament acts ?"
